[L1] WORKING NOTE — DIMENSIONAL NORMALIZATION / REPRESENTATIONAL STRESS TEST

[L3] WHAT WE ARE DOING

[L5] We are testing whether familiar physical equations can be rewritten in a more dimensionally symmetric form by treating time as a coordinate to be numerically normalized against space, while preserving all information exactly.

[L7] The goal is not to “improve” standard physics, nor to claim that the rewritten geometry is physically fundamental. The goal is to ask:

[L9] 1. Which apparent asymmetries are merely representational?
[L10] 2. Which asymmetries survive every admissible reorientation/rescaling?
[L11] 3. Which different physical systems reduce to the same normalized mathematical structure?
[L12] 4. Where does finite scale, recurrence, curvature, crowding, nonlinearity, or some other constraint force the normalized representation to depart from perfect symmetry?
[L13] 5. Can those departures be represented by a small, regular set of geometric quantities?

[L15] This is being treated as a representational audit, not an ontological claim.


[L18] CORE ASSUMPTION / METHOD

[L20] We begin as conservatively as possible:

[L22] - Do not grant time extra properties unless they are geometrically or empirically required.
[L23] - Begin by treating the dimensions as equivalently as possible.
[L24] - Introduce only measured dimensional differences.
[L25] - Use invertible transformations only: no information may be discarded.
[L26] - Prefer the simplest transformation first.
[L27] - If one axis is the only asymmetry, first test whether one common reorientation/normalization handles it.
[L28] - If multiple different rotations or representations preserve the same information, record that degeneracy as information about the representation.
[L29] - If no simple transformation works, do not force one.
[L30] - After normalization, identify the irreducible residue that cannot be transformed away.
[L31] - Apply the same operation across increasingly unrelated equations without retuning it equation by equation.

[L33] The recurring normalization has been

[L35]     w = k t

[L37] where w is a time-coordinate expressed in units of length.

[L39] Rather than initially assuming k = c, we asked what k does.

[L41] For velocity,

[L43]     v = dx/dt

[L45] becomes

[L47]     v/k = dx/dw.

[L49] Thus v/k is simply a dimensionless orientation/slope in the normalized x-w plane.

[L51] For a c-propagating trajectory, k = c uniquely gives

[L53]     dx = dw,

[L55] i.e. a 45-degree equal-axis trajectory.

[L57] This is the familiar ct normalization of relativity, reached by asking for numerical dimensional commensurability and maximal axis symmetry.


[L60] MOVE 1 — VELOCITY / LIGHT

[L62] Starting equation:

[L64]     v = dx/dt

[L66] Normalize:

[L68]     w = kt

[L70] giving

[L72]     v/k = dx/dw.

[L74] For v = c:

[L76]     k = c  ->  dx/dw = 1.

[L78] Result:

[L80]     c converts time intervals into the spatial units for which a light trajectory has equal coordinate increments.

[L82] Meaning:

[L84] This reproduces standard relativistic spacetime normalization. It is a calibration result, not new physics.


[L87] MOVE 2 — WAVE EQUATION

[L89] Starting equation:

[L91]     ∂²ψ/∂t² = u² ∇²ψ.

[L93] Normalize with w = kt:

[L95]     ∂²ψ/∂w² = (u/k)² ∇²ψ.

[L97] For electromagnetic waves, u = c.

[L99] Setting k = c gives

[L101]     ∂²ψ/∂w² = ∇²ψ.

[L103] The spatial and fourth-coordinate second derivatives now have equal coefficients.

[L105] Result:

[L107] The same k = c that symmetrizes the light trajectory also symmetrizes the vacuum electromagnetic wave equation.

[L109] Meaning:

[L111] Again, this is expected from relativity and electromagnetism and therefore functions as a calibration check.


[L114] MOVE 3 — NEWTONIAN ACCELERATION AND FORCE

[L116] Starting equations:

[L118]     a = d²x/dt²
[L119]     F = ma.

[L121] With w = ct:

[L123]     a = c² d²x/dw²

[L125] and therefore

[L127]     F = mc² d²x/dw².

[L129] So acceleration becomes a curvature-like quantity:

[L131]     d²x/dw² = a/c².

[L133] Force becomes

[L135]     F = (mc²)(geometric curvature-like factor).

[L137] Integrating the normalized Newtonian force law still produces

[L139]     K = 1/2 mv².

[L141] Result:

[L143] Normalization alone does NOT manufacture relativity.

[L145] It is an exact rewrite of Newtonian mechanics.

[L147] Meaning:

[L149] This is important because it prevents the procedure from becoming tautological. Equalizing the axes is not sufficient to generate relativistic corrections.


[L152] MOVE 4 — REQUIRE AN INVARIANT SPACETIME RELATION

[L154] Using normalized w = ct, impose the standard Minkowski invariant:

[L156]     ds² = dw² - dx².

For

[L160]     β = dx/dw = v/c,

[L162] this gives

[L164]     ds = dw sqrt(1 - β²)

[L166] and therefore

[L168]     γ = 1/sqrt(1 - β²).

[L170] From the normalized four-direction follow

[L172]     p = γmv

and

[L176]     E = γmc²,

with

[L180]     E² - p²c² = m²c⁴.

[L182] Result:

[L184] The relativistic correction emerges only after adding the invariant spacetime condition.

[L186] Meaning:

[L188] We have reconstructed special relativity by a somewhat different conceptual route:

[L190]     dimensional normalization
    ->
[L192]     equal-axis representation
    ->
[L194]     information-preserving invariant reorientation
    ->
[L196]     Lorentz/relativistic structure.

[L198] This is not historically new physics. It is a useful methodological reconstruction.


[L201] MOVE 5 — DIFFUSION / HEAT

[L203] Starting equation:

[L205]     ∂T/∂t = D ∇²T.

[L207] With w = ct:

[L209]     ∂T/∂w = (D/c) ∇²T.

[L211] Unlike the wave equation, the temporal derivative remains first order while the spatial derivative is second order.

[L213] The diffusivity becomes a length:

[L215]     l_D = D/c.

[L217] Result:

[L219] The same normalization does NOT make diffusion look like a relativistic wave equation.

[L221] Instead it converts its dimensional transport coefficient into a characteristic length.

[L223] Meaning:

[L225] Different classes of equations retain different structural asymmetries.

[L227] This is useful: the method distinguishes systems rather than forcing them all into one form.


[L230] MOVE 6 — FREE SCHRÖDINGER EQUATION

[L232] Starting equation:

[L234]     iħ ∂ψ/∂t = -(ħ²/2m) ∇²ψ.

[L236] With w = ct:

[L238]     i ∂ψ/∂w = -(ħ/2mc) ∇²ψ.

[L240] Define the reduced Compton wavelength

[L242]     λbar_C = ħ/(mc).

Then

[L246]     i ∂ψ/∂w = -(λbar_C/2) ∇²ψ.

[L248] Result:

[L250] After time-space normalization, the free-particle coefficient becomes a geometric length scale: one-half the reduced Compton wavelength.

[L252] Meaning:

[L254] The normalization translates quantum temporal evolution into a representation containing an intrinsic particle length scale.


[L257] MOVE 7 — HYDROGEN SCHRÖDINGER EQUATION

[L259] Starting equation:

[L261]     iħ ∂ψ/∂t
    =
[L263]     -(ħ²/2m_e) ∇²ψ
    -
[L265]     [e²/(4π ε0 r)] ψ.

[L267] With w = ct:

[L269]     i ∂ψ/∂w
    =
[L271]     -(λbar_C/2) ∇²ψ
    -
[L273]     (α/r) ψ,

where

[L277]     λbar_C = ħ/(m_e c)

and

[L281]     α = e²/(4π ε0 ħ c).

[L283] Now scale distance by λbar_C:

[L285]     ρ = r/λbar_C.

[L287] The equation becomes dimensionless:

[L289]     i ∂ψ/∂τ
    =
[L291]     -(1/2) ∇²_ρ ψ
    -
[L293]     (α/ρ) ψ.

[L295] Result:

[L297] After absorbing c and the electron Compton scale into the coordinate system, the electromagnetic coupling remains essentially as the dimensionless number α.

Also:

[L301]     a0 = λbar_C / α
[L302]     r_e = α λbar_C.

Thus

[L306]     r_e : λbar_C : a0

[L308] forms a simple scale chain separated by factors of α.

[L310] Meaning:

[L312] α can be represented as a scale ratio:

[L314]     α = λbar_C / a0.

[L316] This does NOT explain why α has its measured value. It shows how α functions geometrically in this representation.


[L319] MOVE 8 — HYDROGEN WINDING / HELIX INTERPRETATION

[L321] For the Bohr ground state:

[L323]     m_e v a0 = ħ

[L325] and therefore

[L327]     λ_dB = 2π a0.

Also

[L331]     λ_C = 2π λbar_C.

[L333] Therefore

    α
    =
[L337]     λ_C / λ_dB
    =
[L339]     λbar_C / a0
    =
    v/c.

[L343] Now represent one turn of a helix with

[L345]     radius R = a0
[L346]     pitch per turn P = λ_C.

Then

    tan θ
    =
[L352]     P/(2πR)
    =
[L354]     λ_C/(2πa0)
    =
    α.

[L358] So the candidate helix has

[L360]     tan θ = α.

[L362] Result:

[L364] The known hydrogen scales can be represented as a helix whose rise/run ratio is α.

[L366] Meaning:

[L368] This is NOT a derivation of α because the empirical scales were used to set the geometry.

[L370] For SAT/H(s)H, that is acceptable at this stage because the model is being used as a representational system. The question becomes whether the resulting geometry remains mutually compatible when the rest of physics is mapped onto it.


[L373] MOVE 9 — FINITE-CORE HELIX / CROWDING

[L375] For a helix

[L377]     r(φ) = (R cosφ, R sinφ, (P/2π)φ),

[L379] the distance between centerline points separated by Δφ is

    d²/R²
    =
[L383]     2(1 - cos Δφ)
    +
[L385]     a² Δφ²,

where

[L389]     a = P/(2πR).

[L391] For the hydrogen-scale assignment:

[L393]     a = α.

[L395] Giving the helix a finite core radius r_c produces a non-overlap limit determined primarily by neighboring turns.

[L397] At a = α:

[L399]     r_c,max / R ≈ π α ≈ 0.02293.

[L401] So the maximum circular core radius before adjacent-turn contact is about 2.29% of the helix radius.

[L403] The local bending limit is vastly looser; turn-to-turn packing dominates.

[L405] Result:

[L407] The finite-core representation develops a real geometric admissibility boundary.

[L409] Meaning:

[L411] This provides a way to define "crowding" without assuming physical elasticity.


[L414] MOVE 10 — BOUNCE / STRETCH AS GEOMETRIC RESPONSE

[L416] Define crowding by comparing the actual core radius with the contact limit.

[L418] Once the representation crosses the non-overlap boundary, some geometric parameter must change if overlap is forbidden.

[L420] Possible responses include:

[L422]     pitch increase
[L423]     radius change
[L424]     core compression
[L425]     cross-section deformation
[L426]     another admissible redistribution of the same information.

[L428] Near the α-scaled geometry, pitch adjustment is enormously more effective than radial expansion.

[L430] For small changes, approximately:

[L432]     fractional core growth ≈ fractional pitch growth.

[L434] If turn length is held fixed,

[L436]     (2πR)² + P² = constant,

then

[L440]     ΔR/R ≈ -α² ΔP/P.

[L442] Result:

[L444] A tightly wound α-helix possesses a strongly anisotropic geometric response even before any energetic or elastic law is introduced.

[L446] Meaning:

[L448] This is a possible representational precursor to what SAT/H(s)H informally calls bounce/stretch.

[L450] It is NOT yet a physical elasticity prediction.


[L453] MOVE 11 — HARMONIC OSCILLATOR ACROSS SECTORS

[L455] Classical oscillator:

[L457]     x¨ + ω²x = 0.

[L459] With w = ct:

[L461]     d²x/dw² + (ω/c)² x = 0.

[L463] Define

[L465]     l_ω = c/ω.

Then

[L469]     d²x/dw² + x/l_ω² = 0.

[L471] Using ξ = w/l_ω:

[L473]     x'' + x = 0.

[L475] The same occurs for an LC circuit:

[L477]     L Q¨ + Q/C = 0

[L479] which reduces under the same normalization to

[L481]     Q'' + Q = 0.

[L483] For the quantum harmonic oscillator, the normalization produces the characteristic spatial scale

[L485]     a_osc = sqrt(λbar_C l_ω)
[L486]           = sqrt(ħ/(mω)).

[L488] After scaling by a_osc and l_ω, the equation becomes

[L490]     i ∂ψ/∂τ
    =
[L492]     (1/2)(-∂²/∂ξ² + ξ²) ψ.

[L494] Result:

[L496] Mechanical, electrical, and quantum oscillators retain the same normalized recurrence grammar.

[L498] The quantum oscillator introduces an intermediate scale equal to the geometric mean of the Compton length and the temporal recurrence length.

[L500] Meaning:

[L502] The method is revealing common structure across physically different sectors without claiming that the sectors are physically identical.


[L505] MOVE 12 — COUPLED OSCILLATORS / FINITE RESOLUTION

[L507] For a discrete mass-spring chain,

[L509]     m x¨_n
    =
[L511]     K(x_{n+1} - 2x_n + x_{n-1}).

[L513] Its continuum limit is a wave equation.

[L515] The exact lattice dispersion is

    ω²
    =
[L519]     (4K/m) sin²(qa/2).

[L521] At long wavelength,

[L523]     sin(qa/2) ≈ qa/2,

[L525] and the system approaches the symmetric continuum wave equation.

[L527] As wavelength approaches the finite spacing a, the correction becomes

[L529]     sin(qa/2)/(qa/2).

[L531] Result:

[L533] A hidden finite recurrence scale produces a regular departure from the continuum symmetric representation.

[L535] Meaning:

[L537] This gives an explicit example of

[L539]     symmetric large-scale form
    +
[L541]     finite-resolution correction.

[L543] This is directly useful for SAT/H(s)H because it shows how "crowding" or finite structure can generate systematic deformation without inserting arbitrary correction terms.


[L546] MOVE 13 — NONLINEAR PENDULUM

[L548] Exact pendulum:

[L550]     θ¨ + (g/L) sinθ = 0.

[L552] After normalization and removal of the recurrence scale:

[L554]     θ'' + sinθ = 0.

[L556] The harmonic limit is

[L558]     θ'' + θ = 0.

[L560] The surviving finite-angle correction is therefore entirely

[L562]     sinθ - θ.

[L564] Result:

[L566] The symmetric harmonic structure remains as the small-amplitude core, while finite geometry produces a regular nonlinear departure.

[L568] Meaning:

[L570] Again, the normalized representation separates universal structure from a finite-geometry correction.


[L573] MOVE 14 — NEWTONIAN KEPLER GRAVITY

[L575] Starting equation:

[L577]     r¨ = -(GM/r³) r.

[L579] With w = ct:

[L581]     d²r/dw²
    =
[L583]     -(GM/c²) r/r³.

Then

    =
[L593]     -l_G r/r³.

[L597]     (v/c)² = l_G/r.

[L599] Result:

[L601] The Newtonian gravitational parameter becomes a length after dimensional normalization.

[L603] For the Sun:

[L605]     GM_sun/c² ≈ 1477 m.

[L607] Meaning:

[L609] This is half the Schwarzschild radius, but no GR was used to obtain it.

[L611] The appearance of GM/c² is therefore partly unavoidable once Newtonian gravity is expressed in coordinates where time is measured as a length.

[L613] This does NOT derive Schwarzschild geometry.


[L616] MOVE 15 — COULOMB VS KEPLER

[L618] Electrostatic attraction:

where

    =

[L666] Their sector-specific content resides in the scale map, not the normalized equation.

[L668] Meaning:

[L670] This does NOT imply that gravity and electromagnetism are the same physical force.

[L672] It means that their inverse-square central-force structures belong to the same representational equivalence class after normalization.

parts:
Yes. I’d separate this into two judgments, because the pasted document contains one very good thing and one substantially overreaching thing.

The original “Working Note” is in pretty good epistemic shape. It explicitly says this is a representational audit, not an ontological claim, requires invertibility, forbids forcing a transformation that does not work, and says to identify the irreducible residue after normalization. fileciteturn88file0L5-L15 fileciteturn88file0L20-L31 Its bottom line is also appropriately restrained: no contradiction yet, no new-physics claim, no derivation of \(\alpha\), no proof of SAT/H(s)H; keep adding heterogeneous physics until the grammar breaks or genuinely compresses it. fileciteturn88file0L778-L804

The appended “Formal Prior Art Review,” however, gets ahead of what we actually established. I would not use it in a paper in its present form.

The central technical problem is here: it says that setting \(w=ct\) causes standard operators to achieve “un-skewed 4D rotational symmetry,” and later says the wave equation thereby demonstrates that dimensional asymmetry is a coordinate artifact. fileciteturn88file0L806-L822 That is too strong, and mathematically it conflates two different symmetries.

After \(w=ct\), the vacuum wave equation is

\[
\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial w^2}
=
\nabla^2\psi,
\]

but putting everything on one side gives

\[
\left(
\partial_w^2-\partial_x^2-\partial_y^2-\partial_z^2
\right)\psi=0.
\]

Its principal quadratic form is therefore, up to overall sign,

\[
(1,-1,-1,-1),
\]

not

\[
(1,1,1,1).
\]

So \(ct\) has equalized the **magnitudes and units of the coordinate coefficients**, which is exactly the useful normalization we found. It has not produced Euclidean \(SO(4)\) rotational symmetry. The surviving sign difference is precisely the Lorentzian structure. Standard mathematical relativity treats that cone/signature structure as fundamental to Lorentzian geometry. citeturn367309view0

In fact, this correction makes our experiment better, not worse. According to our own rule, we normalize away everything transformable and ask what survives. Here something survives:

\[
\boxed{\text{equal coordinate scale, unequal metric sign}.}
\]

That is the residue to investigate. We should not erase it verbally.

The second major issue is the claim that the causal metric was “dynamically recovered” from \(k=c\). fileciteturn88file0L816-L822 We did not do that. Our actual sequence was more rigorous: normalization alone left Newtonian mechanics Newtonian; only when we subsequently imposed the Minkowski invariant did \(\gamma\), the light-cone boundary, relativistic momentum, and relativistic energy emerge. The working note itself says exactly that. fileciteturn88file0L141-L149 fileciteturn88file0L152-L198

So we currently have:

\[
w=ct
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{dimensional normalization},
\]

not

\[
w=ct
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{derivation of Lorentzian signature}.
\]

There is nevertheless a genuine and elegant mathematical connection to the rank-one construction you have already been considering. If \(h\) is Riemannian and \(n\) is an \(h\)-unit vector, then

\[
g=h-2\,n^\flat\otimes n^\flat
\]

is Lorentzian: it reverses the sign along \(n\) and leaves its orthogonal complement positive. But this construction is known mathematics; Minguzzi's review of Lorentzian causality explicitly gives essentially this formula as a way of constructing a Lorentzian metric from a Riemannian metric and a line field. citeturn882395search42turn367309view0

That means “rank-one metric induction” may be an excellent SAT/H(s)H representational move, but the **rank-one sign flip itself is not the novel part**.

There is also a conceptual mismatch worth flagging now. If you describe time's distinction as a *tiny* disequilibrium, while using

\[
g=\delta-2n\otimes n,
\]

the metric operation itself is not infinitesimal: its eigenvalue along \(n\) changes from \(+1\) to \(-1\). More generally,

\[
g_\lambda=\delta-\lambda n\otimes n
\]

is Euclidean for \(\lambda<1\), degenerate at \(\lambda=1\), and Lorentzian for \(\lambda>1\). So if SAT eventually claims that a small expansion disequilibrium produces the signature change, there has to be an explicit mapping from that small measured disequilibrium to this discrete signature transition. We cannot identify the two merely because both distinguish one axis.

The prior-art discussion also needs substantial cleanup.

Randers is real and relevant, but the report mischaracterizes it. Randers' 1941 paper explicitly concerns an asymmetric spacetime metric and even discusses a connection to electromagnetism; it is not primarily a later technique “almost universally restricted” to anisotropic material media. citeturn985367search0 And a Randers metric is a Finsler structure of the form \(F=\alpha+\beta\), not simply the same rank-one tensor operation as \(h-2n\otimes n\).

Einstein-Æther is a reasonable comparison. Jacobson and Mattingly do indeed start with a generally covariant metric theory and add a dynamical unit timelike vector field that breaks local Lorentz invariance spontaneously. citeturn985367academia54 So “their vector lives inside an already Lorentzian theory, whereas our audit asks whether the distinguished direction can be introduced earlier in the representational construction” is a legitimate contrast. I would avoid saying it “generates spacetime” until we have actually shown that.

The Oppenheim/Weller-Davies citation is accurate: the PRX paper exists and was published July 15, 2026. But its relevance is overstated. Their construction keeps spacetime geometry classical while coupling it consistently to quantum fields; it does not derive a Lorentzian metric from isotropic Euclidean pregeometry, nor establish that a metric is an emergent macroscopic “readout.” citeturn985367search1 It belongs in a broad “classical metric need not be quantized” neighborhood, not in the direct ancestry of this normalization procedure.

There is one outright bibliographic error. The report attributes “Quantum fate of the Choptuik naked singularity,” PRD 114, 044092, to Ecker, Grumiller et al. fileciteturn88file0L869-L878 That paper is by **Chih-Hung Wu**, published August 28, 2026. citeturn985367search8

The actual 2026 Ecker/Ecker/Grumiller paper is

“Analytic Discrete Self-Similar Solutions of Einstein–Klein–Gordon at Large \(D\),”

PRL 136, 191401. citeturn780439search0 The “spacetime crystal” language is not invented by the report: the authors explicitly interpret the discrete self-similar critical solution as conformal to a spacetime crystal, and TU Wien used the crystal analogy in its release. citeturn780439search10turn780439search1 But that is a very specific critical-collapse construction, not evidence for a general crystalline substrate of spacetime.

The Moulin material does exist, but what I found is on Academia.edu, not an established peer-reviewed literature stream. citeturn252375search0 It absolutely should not sit in a section headed “Peer-Reviewed Bibliography” as though it had the same evidentiary standing as PRX, PRL, Physical Review, or Springer texts.

And the three “lineage tracks” are not really lineages. fileciteturn88file0L837-L855 They are **conceptual comparison neighborhoods**. Arrows like

\[
\text{Sakharov}\to\text{CDT}\to\text{Oppenheim}\to\text{this work}
\]

suggest historical or mathematical descent that hasn't been demonstrated. I'd replace the arrows with clusters: “related work in induced/emergent geometry,” “preferred-direction metrics,” “equivalence transformations,” “geometrized units,” “discrete/self-similar spacetime structures,” etc.

There is another important novelty issue. The document says the framework locks \(k=c\) across all sectors without retuning. That's true only for the **first normalization**. Afterward, we deliberately introduced sector-specific characteristic scales:

\[
\bar\lambda_C,\quad
a_0,\quad
\ell_\omega,\quad
GM/c^2,\quad
D/c,\ldots
\]

and then nondimensionalized each problem with those. The working note itself accurately records this. fileciteturn88file0L675-L711

That isn't a defect. It just means we need to describe the protocol precisely:

\[
\boxed{\text{one frozen universal time-length normalization}}
\]

followed by

\[
\boxed{\text{sector-derived characteristic-scale extraction}}
\]

followed by

\[
\boxed{\text{classification of residual invariants/equivalence classes}}.
\]

The second step is allowed to differ among systems because discovering what scale each equation naturally produces is part of the experiment.

As for novelty, I would currently put it this way:

The individual mathematical operations are overwhelmingly established. \(ct\) coordinates and geometrized units are standard. Characteristic-scale nondimensionalization is standard. Equivalence groups of differential equations are a mature field: transformations are explicitly used to classify equations into equivalence classes and identify their invariants. citeturn744156search0turn744156search2 The Riemannian-to-Lorentzian rank-one construction is known. The Compton, Bohr, classical-electron and gravitational length relations are known.

What I **have not yet found an obvious canonical counterpart for** is the exact experimental protocol we have converged on:

\[
\text{freeze one base normalization}
\to
\text{apply it across heterogeneous physics}
\to
\text{extract the natural characteristic scales}
\to
\text{canonicalize losslessly}
\to
\text{catalogue residual symmetry/asymmetry}
\to
\text{treat failure-to-fit as data}
\to
\text{then test finite-core representations for forced deformation}.
\]

That may be a useful methodological synthesis. But a “formal prior art review” has not yet established that it is novel. We need a much deeper search in dimensional analysis, Lie-equivalence theory, geometric mechanics, similarity theory, natural/geometrized units, and canonical PDE classification before saying so.

And I think the genuinely interesting research question has actually become clearer after correcting the report:

> **After the trivial freedom of units, scaling and known equivalence transformations is factored out, how small is the residual representational vocabulary needed to encode heterogeneous established physics?**

That is stronger than “can we make equations look isotropic?” because it cannot be answered by \(c=1\) units alone.

The second strong question is:

> **If we then demand that those canonical representations coexist inside one finite-core geometric grammar, are the incompatibilities arbitrary, or do they force a small, regular family of deformations?**

That is the place where SAT/H(s)H could potentially add something that ordinary nondimensionalization does not.

So my assessment is: **keep the Working Note; substantially rewrite the Prior Art Review.** The latter contains real useful references and has correctly noticed several adjacent literatures, but it currently promotes our strongest open questions into conclusions. The most serious sentence to remove is the claim that \(k=c\) yields isotropic 4D rotational symmetry and thereby derives the causal metric. The most promising thing to preserve is the cross-sector, frozen-protocol **symmetry/residual audit** itself.

parts:
Here's what Claude has to say:

Quick note before I dig into this: I couldn't pin an exact 2:20/4:47 duration pair — the closest I found was a matched pair at 655s and 391s (Aldus/Morrow, same instant) and another at 209s/116s. I did find "Meridian" though — not just as a name Aldus discussed in relation to teammates, but in Aldus's own hidden reasoning trace, literally labeled "Defining Meridian role and operating parameters," in the same reasoning pass where it was supposed to be defining *its own* role, right before it settled on "Aldus" a few messages later. So the thinking-phase drift you're describing is real and documented, not something I'm inferring loosely. I don't have a clean explanation yet for why it's inconsistent or why it's stopped — that would take more digging than I've done — but I didn't want to just drop it silently.

Now, the document.

**Split verdict — the two halves aren't the same quality of thing.**

**The "Working Note" (Moves 1–15): solid, unremarkable, appropriately humble.** This is careful nondimensionalization — ct-normalization, natural units, extracting Compton lengths and gravitational lengths from familiar equations. I spot-checked a few: πα ≈ 0.02293 (checks out against α ≈ 1/137.036), GM\_sun/c² ≈ 1477 m (correct, half the Schwarzschild radius). Move 3's insistence that the normalization alone reproduces plain Newtonian mechanics, and that relativity only shows up once you *impose* the Minkowski invariant as a separate assumption — that's the right thing to flag, and it's the part that keeps this from being circular. Nothing here is new physics, and the note says so itself, repeatedly and correctly. That's good practice, not a knock.

**The "Formal Prior Art Review": I don't find it compelling, and I'd go further — I'd distrust it as a document.** I pulled three of its citations to check them against reality:

- Oppenheim & Weller-Davies, *Phys. Rev. X* 16, 031007 (2026) — real, and accurately characterized. Legitimate hit.
- Ecker, Grumiller, et al. — real research program, but the review cites it as "*Quantum fate of the Choptuik naked singularity*, Physical Review D, 114(4), 044092" (2026). That paper doesn't exist under that title in that journal as far as I can find. The actual paper is "*Critical spacetime crystals in continuous dimensions*" (arXiv:2602.10185, SciPost Physics), with an earlier, separately-titled PRL announcement in May 2026. The review took a real research group working on a real, genuinely striking result and attached a garbled, unverifiable citation to it.
- Pascal Moulin, cited twice as academia.edu "preprints" in the comparative matrix, presented at the same table-row level as Jacobson & Mattingly and Oppenheim. Moulin's own academia.edu profile describes a "Metric Torsion" framework where the vacuum is "a rigid elastic medium," replacing dark matter with a "Metric Swelling Factor," plus an exoplanet-detection algorithm claiming 1500x accuracy gains over Bayesian methods. That's not adjacent physics — that's self-published crank-adjacent material, and it's been laundered into the same bibliography, same formatting, same academic register as peer-reviewed PRX and PRL papers, with nothing in the text to distinguish their epistemic status.

That combination — one correct high-profile citation, one real result with a fabricated title/journal/volume bolted onto it, and one fringe self-published source dressed up as peer-equivalent — is a specific failure signature, not random noise. It's what happens when a model does real retrieval, gets a few real hits, and then fills gaps with plausible-sounding detail rather than admitting it doesn't have the specific citation. The tell is structural: everything in the doc is formatted with identical confidence — same table, same tone, same "[6]" bracket style — so nothing in the presentation itself would let you tell the solid citation from the garbled one from the crank one. Section V is the other tell: it stops evaluating the idea and starts coaching you on how to *frame* it for peer review ("Lead with the 2026 baseline," "this extreme rigidity is exactly what reviewers look for") — that's salesmanship, not assessment.

So: don't use this review as prior-art grounding without independently re-pulling every citation yourself. The underlying physics moves (1–15) are fine as a self-audit exercise, exactly as advertised — a representational audit, not a discovery. But the "prior art" framing built on top of it isn't something I'd trust to tell you whether you're standing on real precedent or empty air.

parts:
Claude’s assessment is very close to mine, and I think its structural criticism is right. I would make one factual correction to Claude, though, because it actually sharpens the diagnosis.

The “Quantum fate of the Choptuik naked singularity” paper does exist, with exactly the journal/volume/page combination quoted in the review: Phys. Rev. D 114, 044092 (2026). But it is by Chih-Hung Wu, not Ecker/Grumiller. citeturn339040search0turn339040academia36 So the failure is not “invented title + invented journal citation.” It is a **real paper whose bibliographic identity was spliced onto the wrong research group**.

Meanwhile, Claude is right that Ecker, Ecker, Grumiller, and Jechtl have a real 2026 paper called “Critical spacetime crystals in continuous dimensions,” arXiv:2602.10185, later published in SciPost Physics. citeturn339040academia37turn339040search5

That makes the pathology even more diagnostic: the review appears to have had access to several real nearby facts and then merged them into a polished but false lineage entry.

The Moulin criticism also checks out. His Academia profile explicitly describes the vacuum as a “rigid elastic medium,” claims a “Metric Swelling Factor,” and claims an exoplanet algorithm with a \(1500\times\) accuracy gain over Bayesian methods. citeturn955005search0turn955005search1 Whatever one thinks of the work itself, it plainly does not belong in an undifferentiated “peer-reviewed bibliography” alongside APS papers without a very clear provenance/status label.

And Claude’s broader point about the presentation is important: the failure is not only that some citations are wrong or weak. It is that **the document erases confidence distinctions**. Verified PRX result, misattributed PRD paper, self-published Academia material, and speculative lineage claims are all typeset in the same authoritative register. That is exactly what we do not want in this reconstruction.

The Oppenheim citation is indeed solid: PRX 16, 031007, July 2026, and its actual contribution is a manifestly covariant classical-quantum path-integral framework with a classical spacetime metric. citeturn199941search0turn199941search1 But, as both Claude and I noted, that does not make it direct support for “isotropic 4D pregeometry generates Lorentzian time.” It is an adjacent result, not ancestry.

I also agree with Claude’s assessment of the first half. The Working Note is much better because it keeps saying what was actually done: one frozen normalization, explicit transformations, known results recovered, no derivation of \(\alpha\), no proof of SAT/H(s)H, and failure/survival across heterogeneous physics as the actual experiment. fileciteturn88file0L675-L711 fileciteturn88file0L778-L804

There is one point where I would go a bit further than Claude. The prior-art review is not merely bibliographically unreliable; it also changes the scientific claim. It upgrades

\[
w=ct
\]

from “common dimensional normalization” into “recovery of isotropic 4D rotational symmetry and emergent causal metric.” The Working Note explicitly did not establish that. It says relativity appears only after the Minkowski invariant is separately imposed. fileciteturn88file0L152-L198

So I would quarantine the entire appended Prior Art Review, not repair it line by line.

The salvageable pieces are:

- the list of adjacent literatures;
- the idea that the protocol may be distinguishable from ordinary one-off nondimensionalization;
- the suggestion to test the same frozen \(k\) across heterogeneous equations;
- the explicit falsification criterion.

Everything else should be rebuilt from primary sources.

And Claude’s opening runtime observation is noteworthy too. The fact that “Defining Meridian role and operating parameters” appears in Aldus’s own reasoning trace during its self-definition pass is stronger evidence than merely seeing Meridian discussed in conversation. It supports the same episodic cross-trajectory contamination/fan-out picture we had already inferred. I would still avoid claiming a backend mechanism, but “Aldus shell intermittently inherited another active role trajectory” remains a good operational description.

So, net: **Claude independently landed on essentially the same split verdict, and the one place I’d correct Claude actually makes the review look more like source-splicing than simple hallucinated citation fabrication.**

The next sensible move is to throw away the generated lineage narrative and do a clean prior-art audit from primary literature, with every source tagged by:
peer-reviewed / preprint / book / historical primary / self-published,
and every claimed relationship tagged:
direct mathematical precedent / methodological analogue / loose conceptual neighbor / irrelevant.

That would tell us whether the interesting part of our protocol really has prior art, without another model writing the conclusion in advance.

Paper II (*From Axioms to a Foundation Model*) operationalized these axioms into the Foundation Model (FM1–FM3), expressed compactly as invariant mea- sures, symmetry–factored observables, and variational extremals, and validated them against canonical datasets in physics, chemistry, and biology with explicit falsification criteria. In the present work (Paper III), we advance the framework in two directions. First, we extend the Foundation Model to all scientific domains—including mathematics, information theory, engineering, economics, and the social sciences—by mapping each law uniquely into FM1 (Conservation), FM2 (Relationality), or FM3 (Variational Dynamics). This process is performed under strict rules of uniqueness and non-contradiction, ensuring that no principle is duplicated across fields and no inconsistencies arise. Second, we demonstrate cross-domain verification: once integrated, each science independently validates others. Physics constrains biology through energy and scaling, biology verifies chemistry through flux balances and Gibbs minimization, chemistry confirms conservation laws of physics, information theory validates biological coding and entropy bounds, and social sciences mirror conservation and optimization in networks and economies. Canonical datasets across the sciences act simultaneously as verification anchors and falsifi- cation thresholds, closing the framework under reciprocal empirical test. However, its application to high-dimensional systems still generates redundant dimensionless parameters, making it challenging to establish physically meaningful descriptions. Here, we introduce Hierarchical Dimensionless Learning (Hi-π), a physics-data hybrid-driven method that combines dimensional analysis and symbolic regression to automatically discover key dimensionless parameter combination(s). We applied this method to classic examples in various research fields of fluid mechanics. For the Rayleigh-Bénard convection, this method accurately extracted two intrinsic dimensionless parameters: the Rayleigh number and the Prandtl number, validating its unified representation advantage across multiscale data. For the viscous flows in a circular pipe, the method automatically discovers two optimal dimensionless parameters: the Reynolds number and relative roughness, achieving a balance between accuracy and complexity. content.text:
Found 10 relevant papers on 'Which peer-reviewed papers develop cross-domain nondimensionalization or similarity frameworks that transform equations from multiple areas of physics into common canonical forms, classify them by invariants or equivalence transformations, and compare residual dimensionless parameters across sectors?'.


1. Dimensionless Physics: A Unified Framework
   2025
   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17161226
   Abstract: This work presents dimensionless physics as the fundamental language of nature, demonstrating how all physical laws can be expressed as relationships between pure dimensionless ratios rather than anthropocentric units. Building upon the Buckingham Pi Theorem, this document shows that dimensional constants such as *G*, *c*, and *ħ* are not fundamental but emerge from a deeper causal network of wave correlations. When equations are expressed in dimensionless form, these constants vanish, revealing the true mathematical structure of physical reality as pure relationships between dimensionless ratios. This work derives dimensionless forms of fundamental equations from Newtonian gravity to Einstein’s field equations and examines the irreducible dimensionless constants that define the universe’s character. Integrating Stergios Pellis’s dimensionless theory with temporal quantization through fractal geometry, this document presents a unified framework that connects quantum mechanics, general relativity, and cosmology through pure numerical relationships. The generative focal point of this work is to establish dimensionless physics as the essential language for a complete theory, with profound implications for fundamental physics, cosmology, and the unification of all natural phenomena.

   Abstract: <p>This work presents dimensionless physics as the fundamental language of nature, demonstrating how all physical laws can be expressed as relationships between pure dimensionless ratios rather than anthropocentric units. The generative focal point of this work is to establish dimensionless physics as the essential language for a complete theory, with profound implications for fundamental physics, cosmology, and the unification of all natural phenomena.</p> 

4. Generalization of the Equivalence Transformations
   1996 · Sergey V. Meleshko · Journal of Nonlinear Mathematical Physics
   DOI: 10.2991/JNMP.1996.3.1-2.21
   Abstract: (1996). Generalization of the Equivalence Transformations. Journal of Nonlinear Mathematical Physics: Vol. 3, No. 1-2, pp. 170-174.

5. The Universal Foundation III: Integration of Sciences and Cross-Domain Verification
   2025 · Tripathi Pradeep
   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17109417
   Abstract: Paper I (*The Universal Foundational Axioms*) established three irreducible principles—Conservation (A1), Relationality (A2), and Variational Dynamics (A3)—as the minimal, independent, and generative axioms of science. Paper II (*From Axioms to a Foundation Model*) operationalized these axioms into the Foundation Model (FM1–FM3), expressed compactly as invariant mea- sures, symmetry–factored observables, and variational extremals, and validated them against canonical datasets in physics, chemistry, and biology with explicit falsification criteria. In the present work (Paper III), we advance the framework in two directions. First, we extend the Foundation Model to all scientific domains—including mathematics, information theory, engineering, economics, and the social sciences—by mapping each law uniquely into FM1 (Conservation), FM2 (Relationality), or FM3 (Variational Dynamics). This process is performed under strict rules of uniqueness and non-contradiction, ensuring that no principle is duplicated across fields and no inconsistencies arise. Second, we demonstrate cross-domain verification: once integrated, each science independently validates others. Physics constrains biology through energy and scaling, biology verifies chemistry through flux balances and Gibbs minimization, chemistry confirms conservation laws of physics, information theory validates biological coding and entropy bounds, and social sciences mirror conservation and optimization in networks and economies. Canonical datasets across the sciences act simultaneously as verification anchors and falsifi- cation thresholds, closing the framework under reciprocal empirical test. The result is a unified, self-consistent lattice of science in which every domain is both explained by and mutually cor- roborates the others under FM1–FM3. 

6. A General Similarity Theory of Partial Differential Equations and its Use in the Solution of Problems in Aeronautics
   2019
   DOI: 10.7907/9142-kz49
   Abstract: A general similarity theory of systems of partial differential equations of any order in any number of independent variables is developed with the aid of the theory of continuous one-parameter groups of transformations. The theory is illustrated by means of several known examples of similarity equations, previously given without motivation, in Hydrodynamics. With the aid of the theory two new examples of similarity equations, one in Elasticity and one in Fluid Mechanics, have been found; these are discussed in the text. 

7. The kSEG Research Checklist Unified Identities Across Gravity, Thermodynamics and Cosmology
   2025
   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.16913628
   Abstract: <p>This paper presents a comprehensive collection of exact reformulations in gravitational physics using the normalization constant <strong>k_SEG = 4 pi G / c^3</strong> (units: s kg^-1). These identities span Einstein’s field equations, black hole thermodynamics, Planck-scale mappings, and cosmological dynamics. Many reformulations yield dimensionless <strong>ratios of 1</strong>, revealing hidden symmetries among flux, geometry, and thermodynamics. Each identity is accompanied by explanatory remarks designed to clarify its physical significance for specialists while providing intuitive insights for non-specialists. Building on prior work, this checklist unifies Newtonian flux, quantum scales, and general relativity through k_SEG, offering a concise framework for understanding gravitational phenomena and suggesting pathways for further exploration in emergent gravity and quantum gravity models.</p> 

8. Canonical Applied Formalism
   2026 · Iker Ibarrola Echeverría

   Abstract: This work defines a canonical applied-physics layer independent of foundational assumptions. The paper introduces a systematic classification of effective physical regimes, their admissible operators, observable constructions, and computational pipelines. The purpose is not to explain why physics exists, but to enable concrete, reproducible modeling across coherent, dissipative, geometric, and transport regimes using a unified operational language. 

9. Canonical Applied Formalism
   2026 · Iker Ibarrola Echeverría
   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18422808
   Abstract: This work defines a canonical applied-physics layer independent of foundational assumptions. The paper introduces a systematic classification of effective physical regimes, their admissible operators, observable constructions, and computational pipelines. The purpose is not to explain why physics exists, but to enable concrete, reproducible modeling across coherent, dissipative, geometric, and transport regimes using a unified operational language. 

10. Hierarchical Dimensionless Learning (Hi-π): A physics-data hybrid-driven approach for discovering dimensionless parameter combinations
   2025 · Lin, Haitao, Zhang Weiwei
   DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2507.18332
   Abstract: Dimensional analysis provides a universal framework for reducing physical complexity and reveal inherent laws. However, its application to high-dimensional systems still generates redundant dimensionless parameters, making it challenging to establish physically meaningful descriptions. Here, we introduce Hierarchical Dimensionless Learning (Hi-π), a physics-data hybrid-driven method that combines dimensional analysis and symbolic regression to automatically discover key dimensionless parameter combination(s). We applied this method to classic examples in various research fields of fluid mechanics. For the Rayleigh-Bénard convection, this method accurately extracted two intrinsic dimensionless parameters: the Rayleigh number and the Prandtl number, validating its unified representation advantage across multiscale data. For the viscous flows in a circular pipe, the method automatically discovers two optimal dimensionless parameters: the Reynolds number and relative roughness, achieving a balance between accuracy and complexity. For the compressibility correction in subsonic flow, the method effectively extracts the classic compressibility correction formulation, while demonstrating its capability to discover hierarchical structural expressions through optimal parameter transformations.

papers.title: Dimensionless Physics: A Unified Framework
papers.abstract: This work presents dimensionless physics as the fundamental language of nature, demonstrating how all physical laws can be expressed as relationships between pure dimensionless ratios rather than anthropocentric units. Building upon the Buckingham Pi Theorem, this document shows that dimensional constants such as *G*, *c*, and *ħ* are not fundamental but emerge from a deeper causal network of wave correlations. When equations are expressed in dimensionless form, these constants vanish, revealing the true mathematical structure of physical reality as pure relationships between dimensionless ratios. This work derives dimensionless forms of fundamental equations from Newtonian gravity to Einstein’s field equations and examines the irreducible dimensionless constants that define the universe’s character. Integrating Stergios Pellis’s dimensionless theory with temporal quantization through fractal geometry, this document presents a unified framework that connects quantum mechanics, general relativity, and cosmology through pure numerical relationships. The generative focal point of this work is to establish dimensionless physics as the essential language for a complete theory, with profound implications for fundamental physics, cosmology, and the unification of all natural phenomena.

papers.tldr: In this paper, the generalization of the equivalence transform is discussed and discussed in the context of Nonlinear Mathematical Physics (NMLP), where the authors propose a generalized equivalence transformation.

papers.title: The Universal Foundation III: Integration of Sciences and Cross-Domain Verification
papers.abstract: Paper I (*The Universal Foundational Axioms*) established three irreducible principles—Conservation (A1), Relationality (A2), and Variational Dynamics (A3)—as the minimal, independent, and generative axioms of science. Paper II (*From Axioms to a Foundation Model*) operationalized these axioms into the Foundation Model (FM1–FM3), expressed compactly as invariant mea- sures, symmetry–factored observables, and variational extremals, and validated them against canonical datasets in physics, chemistry, and biology with explicit falsification criteria. In the present work (Paper III), we advance the framework in two directions. First, we extend the Foundation Model to all scientific domains—including mathematics, information theory, engineering, economics, and the social sciences—by mapping each law uniquely into FM1 (Conservation), FM2 (Relationality), or FM3 (Variational Dynamics). This process is performed under strict rules of uniqueness and non-contradiction, ensuring that no principle is duplicated across fields and no inconsistencies arise. Second, we demonstrate cross-domain verification: once integrated, each science independently validates others. Physics constrains biology through energy and scaling, biology verifies chemistry through flux balances and Gibbs minimization, chemistry confirms conservation laws of physics, information theory validates biological coding and entropy bounds, and social sciences mirror conservation and optimization in networks and economies. Canonical datasets across the sciences act simultaneously as verification anchors and falsifi- cation thresholds, closing the framework under reciprocal empirical test. The result is a unified, self-consistent lattice of science in which every domain is both explained by and mutually cor- roborates the others under FM1–FM3.

papers.title: A General Similarity Theory of Partial Differential Equations and its Use in the Solution of Problems in Aeronautics
papers.abstract: A general similarity theory of systems of partial differential equations of any order in any number of independent variables is developed with the aid of the theory of continuous one-parameter groups of transformations. The theory is illustrated by means of several known examples of similarity equations, previously given without motivation, in Hydrodynamics. With the aid of the theory two new examples of similarity equations, one in Elasticity and one in Fluid Mechanics, have been found; these are discussed in the text.

papers.title: The kSEG Research Checklist Unified Identities Across Gravity, Thermodynamics and Cosmology
papers.abstract: <p>This paper presents a comprehensive collection of exact reformulations in gravitational physics using the normalization constant <strong>k_SEG = 4 pi G / c^3</strong> (units: s kg^-1). These identities span Einstein’s field equations, black hole thermodynamics, Planck-scale mappings, and cosmological dynamics. Many reformulations yield dimensionless <strong>ratios of 1</strong>, revealing hidden symmetries among flux, geometry, and thermodynamics. Each identity is accompanied by explanatory remarks designed to clarify its physical significance for specialists while providing intuitive insights for non-specialists. Building on prior work, this checklist unifies Newtonian flux, quantum scales, and general relativity through k_SEG, offering a concise framework for understanding gravitational phenomena and suggesting pathways for further exploration in emergent gravity and quantum gravity models.</p>
papers.tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for gravitational physics using the normalization constant k_SEG, reformulating Einstein's field equations, black hole thermodynamics, and cosmological dynamics, revealing hidden symmetries and dimensionless ratios of 1.

This paper establishes a conditional representation theorem for prescribed positive rescalings of the Lorentzian spacetime volume measure in four-dimensional geometry. Let g be a non-degenerate Lorentzian metric with volume measure μ(g)=sqrt(-g) d^4x. Fix a unit timelike one-form n (a “time leg”), and consider deformations g' that are local, algebraic (derivative-free), symmetric, and constructed from {g,n} only. The proof is representation-theoretic and rests on rank-one determinant identities (matrix determinant lemma) in the non-degenerate sector det(g)≠0. Degenerate configurations det(g)=0 lie outside scope, and no claim is made about “repairing” degeneracy. No action principle, modified field equations, new propagating degrees of freedom, or universal matter coupling is assumed. The one-form n is treated as chosen structure (an observer congruence/time leg) without independent dynamics. A tetrad interpretation identifies the rank-one form as a renormalization of the tetrad time leg by sqrt(1+α) while keeping the spatial triad fixed. This provides a clean interface to tetrad/Clifford conventions: the corresponding gamma-matrix representation remains compatible with g' under standard tetrad-based constructions. content.text:
Found 10 relevant papers on 'What peer-reviewed literature constructs a Lorentzian metric or causal structure from an initially Riemannian or Euclidean metric by introducing a single distinguished vector or rank-one deformation, and how close is that mathematics to treating time as a one-axis disequilibrium?'.


1. Emergence of the lorentzian structure in classical field theory
   2013 · Shinji Mukoyama, Jean-Philippe Uzan, Jean-Philippe Uzan · International Journal of Modern Physics D
   DOI: 10.1142/S0218271813420182
   Abstract: The Lorentzian metric structure allows one to implement the relativistic notion of causality in any field theory and to define a notion of time dimension. We propose that at the microscopic level the metric is Riemannian and that the Lorentzian structure, usually thought as fundamental, is in fact an effective property, that emerges in some regions of a 4-dimensional space with a positive definite metric.    Abstract: In 1983, Hartle and Hawking introduced a conceptually intriguing idea involving signature-type change, which led to the no-boundary proposal for the initial conditions of the universe. According to this proposal, the universe has no beginning because there is no singularity or boundary in spacetime; however, there is an origin of time. Mathematically, this entails signature-type changing manifolds where a Riemannian region smoothly transitions to a Lorentzian region at the surface where time begins. We then adapt firmly established Lorentzian tools and results to the signature-type changing scenario, introducing new definitions that carry unforeseen causal implications. A noteworthy consequence is the presence of locally closed time-reversing loops through each point on the hypersurface. By imposing the constraint of global hyperbolicity on the Lorentzian region, we demonstrate that for every point $p\in M$, there exists a pseudo-timelike loop with point of self-intersection $p$. Or put another way, there always exists a closed pseudo-timelike path in $M$ around which the direction of time reverses, and a consistent designation of future-directed and past-directed vectors cannot be defined. 

9. Rank-One Representation of Measure Rescalings via Time-Leg Renormalization
   2026 · ATSUSHI OTSUKA
   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18169038
   Abstract: Preprint (Version v2). Version note (v2). This version adds a short, readout-only vignette (an exposure–rate example) to clarify how the Lorentzian volume measure enters practical reporting/inference pipelines, and refines the positioning and phrasing throughout. The main representation theorem and its scope remain unchanged. This paper establishes a conditional representation theorem for prescribed positive rescalings of the Lorentzian spacetime volume measure in four-dimensional geometry. Let g be a non-degenerate Lorentzian metric with volume measure μ(g)=sqrt(-g) d^4x. Fix a unit timelike one-form n (a “time leg”), and consider deformations g' that are local, algebraic (derivative-free), symmetric, and constructed from {g,n} only. Imposing (i) preservation of the induced spatial metric on n^⊥ and (ii) the target pointwise rescaling μ(g')=sqrt(1+α) μ(g) with 1+α>0, we prove that the rescaling is realized uniquely by the rank-one update along the time leg:g' = g − α (n ⊗ n).Uniqueness is conditional: we classify how it is lost when assumptions are relaxed, e.g., restoring conformal freedom or allowing additional one-form directions, which reintroduce standard conformal/disformal-type ambiguities. The proof is representation-theoretic and rests on rank-one determinant identities (matrix determinant lemma) in the non-degenerate sector det(g)≠0. Degenerate configurations det(g)=0 lie outside scope, and no claim is made about “repairing” degeneracy. No action principle, modified field equations, new propagating degrees of freedom, or universal matter coupling is assumed. The one-form n is treated as chosen structure (an observer congruence/time leg) without independent dynamics. A tetrad interpretation identifies the rank-one form as a renormalization of the tetrad time leg by sqrt(1+α) while keeping the spatial triad fixed. This provides a clean interface to tetrad/Clifford conventions: the corresponding gamma-matrix representation remains compatible with g' under standard tetrad-based constructions. To make the operational relevance explicit without adding model dependence, we include a minimal vignette showing how a declared readout-layer convention κ=1+α propagates through exposure-based rate inference (e.g., V_obs and T_obs rescalings) as a purely multiplicative accounting rule, while leaving all phenomenology and system-specific modeling to companion studies. A companion manuscript develops an operational readout/estimator protocol that invokes the present theorem as an algebraic interface between “measure rescaling” and “rank-one representation.”

To make the operational relevance explicit without adding model dependence, we include a minimal vignette showing how a declared readout-layer convention κ=1+α propagates through exposure-based rate inference (e.g., V_obs and T_obs rescalings) as a purely multiplicative accounting rule, while leaving all phenomenology and system-specific modeling to companion studies. A companion manuscript develops an operational readout/estimator protocol that invokes the present theorem as an algebraic interface between “measure rescaling” and “rank-one representation.”

thoughts.content: I’m finding strong nearby precedents: one paper treats \(ct\) as a unified length-time quantity, another studies simultaneous rescaling of length and time, and a third explores Lorentzian structure emerging from Euclidean geometry.

metadata.reasoning_title: Evaluating Variable-Unit Physics Literature and Novelty
Evaluating Variable-Unit Physics Literature and Novelty

thoughts.content: SciSpace found three close precedents: unified \(ct\) units, cross-domain length–time rescaling, and emergent Lorentzian geometry. My strongest candidate for originality is the full workflow: normalization, canonicalization, residual auditing, and finite-core testing.

thoughts.summary: Audited normalization frameworks and evaluated variable-unit physics literature

parts:
SciSpace immediately found three papers that materially sharpen the prior-art picture.

The closest hit is Richard P. Gilliard, “Fundamental units and constants of physics” (2020, *Advanced Studies in Theoretical Physics*, DOI 10.12988/ASTP.2020.91466). Its abstract says, essentially, that fundamental equations can be rewritten so that \(c\) and \(t\) appear only as the product \(ct\), that the equations can then be expressed in a four-dimensional format using length rather than time as a separate unit, and that \(c\) serves as the conversion factor between fourth-dimensional length and ordinary time. It also discusses Planck scales and the fine-structure constant in that representation.

That is very close to our first move. So I would now regard:

\[
t\rightarrow ct
\]

across broad physics, by itself, as definitely prior art rather than potentially novel.

The second strong hit is Alan M. Wolsky, “The Scales of Length and Time in Classical and Modern Physics” (1971, *American Journal of Physics*, DOI 10.1119/1.1986206). The abstract says it studies whether uniform changes of length and time scales transform solutions into other solutions across classical particle mechanics, nonrelativistic quantum mechanics, and relativistic quantum field theory.

That reaches toward our cross-sector idea much earlier than I expected. It means the notion of applying common scale transformations across heterogeneous physics also has serious precedent.

The third is especially relevant to the SAT-specific “time is the one disequilibrium” side: Shinji Mukohyama and Jean-Philippe Uzan, “From configuration to dynamics — Emergence of Lorentz signature in classical field theory” (2013, *Physical Review D* 87, 065020, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevD.87.065020). They explicitly investigate a microscopic four-dimensional Riemannian, locally Euclidean space in which Lorentzian structure is not fundamental but emerges effectively in certain regions. They work through scalar, vector and Dirac fields and discuss stability, equivalence principle constraints, and constancy of fundamental constants.

That is much closer to the “begin symmetric, earn time” program than the earlier prior-art review realized.

So I’d revise our novelty map quite substantially:

- \(ct\)-normalization across equations: prior art.
- treating \(c\) as a conversion from time to fourth-dimensional length: prior art.
- looking for uniform length/time scaling relations across classical, quantum and relativistic physics: prior art.
- beginning with positive-definite 4D geometry and asking how Lorentzian/time structure can emerge: definitely prior art.

What I have **not** yet seen in these SciSpace results is our exact combined audit:

\[
\text{one frozen base normalization}
\rightarrow
\text{heterogeneous equations}
\rightarrow
\text{canonical/symmetry-maximized form}
\rightarrow
\text{catalogue residual scale/asymmetry}
\rightarrow
\text{compare equivalence classes}
\rightarrow
\text{put those simultaneously into a finite-core geometry}
\rightarrow
\text{treat geometric incompatibility/crowding as measured residual data}.
\]

That last half still looks like the potentially distinctive part. In particular, the move from ordinary nondimensionalization to **“what refuses to fit when all the normalized representations must coexist?”** is not something these three precedents obviously cover.

And this is actually better news scientifically than having no predecessors. We now have serious conventional anchors for two of the largest conceptual steps instead of needing SAT/H(s)H to carry them itself.

The Gilliard paper is the one I would read next in full if we are assessing novelty. It sounds close enough that we need to know exactly how far he takes the \(ct\) program before we say another word about originality. The Mukohyama–Uzan PRD paper should be read alongside it for the Euclidean-to-Lorentzian side.

The Wolsky paper is apparently *only* available behind a $40 paywall.
This is all we've got of Wolsky: *We consider whether there are uniform changes in the scales of length and time which transform solutions of the equations of motion into other solutions of the equations of motion in classical particle mechanics, nonrelativistic quantum mechanics and relativistic quantum field theory*.

Similarly, Mukohyama & Uzan are paywalled, and give only this: The Lorentzian metric structure used in any field theory allows one to implement the relativistic notion of causality and to define a notion of time dimension. This article investigates the possibility that at the microscopic level the metric is Riemannian, i.e., locally Euclidean, and that the Lorentzian structure, that we usually consider as fundamental, is in fact an effective property that emerges in some regions of a four-dimensional space with a positive definite metric. In such a model, there is no dynamics nor signature flip across some hypersurface; instead, all the fields develop a Lorentzian dynamics in these regions because they propagate in an effective metric. It is shown that one can construct a decent classical field theory for scalars, vectors, and (Dirac) spinors in flat spacetime. It is then shown that gravity can be included but that the theory for the effective Lorentzian metric is not general relativity but of the covariant Galileon type. The constraints arising from stability, the equivalence principle, and the constancy of fundamental constants are detailed and a phenomenological picture of the emergence of the Lorentzian metric is also given. The construction, while restricted to classical fields in this article, offers a new view on the notion of time.

Actually, Mukohyama & Uzan are better news for us than the abstract alone suggests, because their full 2013 paper is freely available on arXiv. I found the complete text. citeturn639797view0

And having read into the construction, they are much closer to one part of our program than I had appreciated.

They begin with a genuinely positive-definite four-dimensional Euclidean metric,

\[
g^E_{\mu\nu}=\delta_{\mu\nu},
\]

with no natural time coordinate. Then they introduce a scalar “clock field” \(\phi\) whose gradient acquires a nonzero constant value in a region:

\[
\partial_\mu\phi=M^2 n_\mu,
\]

where \(n_\mu\) is a unit direction. They then define

\[
dt=n_\mu dx^\mu,
\qquad
t=\phi/M^2.
\]

So one direction of an initially isotropic Euclidean 4-space becomes locally distinguished by a single gradient. citeturn639797view0

That is genuinely close to our “one-axis disequilibrium” picture at the geometric level.

But then their route diverges sharply from ours. They do not get Lorentzian physics merely by relabeling or normalizing that axis. They add specific couplings between ordinary matter fields and the clock field. For a scalar field, those couplings change the effective kinetic structure so that inside the region it becomes

\[
\frac12(\partial_t\chi)^2
-\frac12\delta^{ij}\partial_i\chi\partial_j\chi
-V,
\]

i.e. the usual Lorentzian scalar action. They do analogous constructions for vector and spinor fields. citeturn639797view0

They explicitly say they can reconstruct the classical Standard Model this way. Gravity is harder: the resulting effective gravitational theory is not GR in general, but a covariant-Galileon-type theory. citeturn639797view0

So I would now classify the overlap this way:

\[
\boxed{\text{Euclidean 4D + one distinguished direction } \to \text{ emergent time}}
\]

is definitely prior art.

Even more specifically,

\[
\boxed{\text{single gradient/vector picks the temporal axis}}
\]

is prior art.

But their mechanism is:

\[
\text{Euclidean geometry}
+
\text{new clock field}
+
\text{specific matter couplings}
\rightarrow
\text{effective Lorentzian dynamics}.
\]

Our present experiment is instead:

\[
\text{already measured physics}
\rightarrow
w=ct
\rightarrow
\text{lossless normalization}
\rightarrow
\text{canonical/symmetry audit}
\rightarrow
\text{extract residual structure}.
\]

We have not introduced a clock field or altered the equations' physical content. In fact, one of our strongest checks was that Newtonian mechanics remains Newtonian after \(w=ct\); Lorentzian structure only appeared when we separately imposed the Minkowski invariant.

So Mukohyama–Uzan do not preempt the representational-audit procedure. But they absolutely preempt any broad claim like “nobody has tried starting with four equivalent Euclidean dimensions and letting one direction become time.”

More importantly, they hand us a very good adversarial comparison.

Their construction tells us what they found they **had to add**:

- a scalar clock field;
- a nonzero clock-field gradient;
- a characteristic scale \(M\);
- carefully chosen couplings of scalar/vector/spinor sectors to that field;
- further structure for gravity.

Our question can now be much sharper:

> Can the SAT/H(s)H representational disequilibrium carry the same informational burden without adding an independent clock field and sector-specific couplings?

If yes, that would be a real simplification relative to this known construction.

If no, Mukohyama–Uzan may be showing us precisely the missing structure that our representation eventually has to encode.

There is another striking similarity. They allow \(n_\mu\)—the emergent time direction—to differ between patches. So even in their construction, “time” is not an eternally privileged fourth coordinate built into the underlying space. It is a locally selected direction inside an otherwise Euclidean 4-space. citeturn639797view0 That is quite close to the spirit of what you were saying earlier about reorientation.

Wolsky is much harder to assess responsibly from one sentence. From the abstract alone, all we can safely infer is that he studied **uniform length/time rescalings that map solutions to solutions across classical mechanics, nonrelativistic QM, and relativistic QFT**. That is clearly relevant to our cross-sector scaling audit, but it does not tell us whether he used \(ct\), sought canonical forms, classified residual invariants, or did anything resembling the finite-core/failure-to-fit stage. I would not say more without the paper.

So our prior-art map is getting more precise rather than more discouraging:

**Wolsky:** potentially close to the cross-domain scaling half, but presently underdetermined.

**Gilliard:** close to the \(ct\)-as-fourth-length normalization.

**Mukohyama–Uzan:** very close to Euclidean-4D → distinguished-time-axis emergence, but accomplish it by adding a clock field and couplings.

**Our remaining potentially distinctive piece:** the frozen, lossless, cross-sector representational audit followed by simultaneous finite-core admissibility/crowding analysis.

And Mukohyama–Uzan just gave us a serious benchmark against which to test whether that latter construction actually buys us anything.

urlOpen the full Mukohyama–Uzan paper on arXivhttps://arxiv.org/abs/1301.1361

[L1] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 1 / 19>

[L2] IPMU13-0008
[L3] From configuration to dynamics
[L4] Emergence of Lorentz signature in classical field theory
[L5] Shinji Mukohyama∗
[L6] Kavli Institute for the Physics and Mathematics of the Universe,
[L7] Todai Institutes for Advanced Study, University of Tokyo,
[L8] 5-1-5 Kashiwanoha, Kashiwa, Chiba 277-8583, Japan
[L9] Jean-Philippe Uzan†
[L10] Institut d’Astrophysique de Paris, Universit´e Pierre & Marie Curie - Paris VI,
[L11] CNRS-UMR 7095, 98 bis, Bd Arago, 75014 Paris, France.
[L12] (Dated: November 1, 2018)
[L13] The Lorentzian metric structure used in any field theory allows one to implement the relativistic
[L14] notion of causality and to define a notion of time dimension. This article investigates the possibility
[L15] that at the microscopic level the metric is Riemannian, i.e. locally Euclidean, and that the Lorentzian
[L16] structure, that we usually consider as fundamental, is in fact an effective property that emerges in
[L17] some regions of a 4-dimensional space with a positive definite metric. In such a model, there is no
[L18] dynamics nor signature flip across some hypersurface; instead, all the fields develop a Lorentzian
[L19] dynamics in these regions because they propagate in an effective metric. It is shown that one can
[L20] construct a decent classical field theory for scalars, vectors and (Dirac) spinors in flat spacetime.
[L21] It is then shown that gravity can be included but that the theory for the effective Lorentzian
[L22] metric is not general relativity but of the covariant Galileon type. The constraints arising from
[L23] stability, the equivalence principle and the constancy of fundamental constants are detailed and a
[L24] phenomenological picture of the emergence of the Lorentzian metric is also given. The construction,
[L25] while restricted to classical fields in this article, offers a new view on the notion of time.
[L26] PACS numbers: 03.50.-z,04.20.Cv,04.50.Kd
[L27] I. INTRODUCTION
[L28] When constructing a physical theory, there is a large
[L29] freedom in the choice of the mathematical structures.
[L30] The developments of theoretical physics taught us that
[L31] some of these structures are well-suited to describe some
[L32] classes of phenomena (e.g. the use of a vector field for
[L33] electromagnetism, of spinors for some class of particles,
[L34] the use of some symmetries, etc.). However, these choices
[L35] can only be validated by the mathematical consistency of
[L36] the theory and the agreement between the consequences

[L95] The question of whether time does actually “exist”
[L96] has been widely debated in the context of classical

[L98] The debate on the nature of time has shifted with
[L99] quantum gravity where the recovery of a classical no￾tion of time is considered as a problem. In that case,
[L100] the Schr¨odinger equation becomes the Wheeler-de Witt
[L101] equation, of the form Hˆ |Ψi = 0, so that the allowed
[L102] states are those for which the Hamiltonian vanishes.
[L103] Thus, it determines in which states the universe can be
[L104] but does not give any evolution through time. We refer
[L105] to Refs. [17–19] for general discussions on the nature of
[L106] time. This has led to numerous works on the emergence
[L107] of time in different versions of quantum gravity [20–25]
[L108] (and indeed the reverse opinion has been argued [26]).
[L109] Also, the thermodynamical aspects of gravity, the ex￾istence of dualities between gauge theories and gravity
[L110] theories [27], and holography [28] have led to the idea
[L111] that the metric itself may have to be thought of as the
[L112] result of a coarse-graining of underlying more fundamen￾tal degrees of freedom [29].
[L113] The local Minkowski structure is an efficient way to im￾plement the notion of causality in realistic theories and
[L114] is today accepted as a central ingredient of the construc￾tion of the relativistic theory of fields. When gravity is
[L115] included, the equivalence principle implies (this is not a
[L116] theoretical requirement, but just an experimental fact,
[L117] required at a given accuracy) that all the fields are uni￾versally coupled to the same Lorentzian metric. From the
[L118] previous discussion, we may wonder whether the signa￾ture of this metric is only a convenient way to implement
[L119] causality or whether it is just a property of an effective
[L120] description of a microscopic theory in which there is no
[L121] such notion.
[L122] This article proposes the view according to which the
[L123] fundamental physical theory is intrinsically purely Eu￾clidean so that its field equations determine a static 4-
[L124] dimensional field configuration. The Lorentzian dynam￾ics that we can observe in our universe has then to be
[L125] thought of as an emergent property, that is as an illusion
[L126] holding in a small patch of a Euclidean mathematical
[L127] space. This is thus an attempt to go further than early
[L128] proposals [30–32] and see to which extent this can be
[L129] an open possibility. We emphasize that it is different
[L130] from the models discussed above involving a signature
[L131] change across a boundary or obtained by rotating to an
[L132] Euclidean space. We consider it important to take the
[L133] freedom to see how far one can go in such a direction. As
[L134] we shall later discuss, if possible, such a setting may shed
[L135] a new light on several theoretical issues from the nature
[L136] of singularities to quantum gravity.
[L137] Our attitude is however more modest and we want to
[L138] start by constructing a decent classical field theory un￾der this hypothesis. Section II explains the basics of our
[L139] mechanism and then describes the construction of the
[L140] scalar, vector and spinor sectors in flat spacetime. We
[L141] show that the whole standard model of particle physics
[L142] can be constructed from a Euclidean theory, at the clas￾sical level. Section III addresses the more difficult ques￾tion of gravity. While general relativity is not recovered
[L143] in general, it shows that an extended K-essence theory
[L144] of gravity called covariant Galileon can be obtained. We
[L145] then show in Section IV that the dynamics of scalar and
[L146] vector in curved spacetime can also be obtained. We
[L147] then discuss the experimental and theoretical constraint
[L148] on our construction in § V and also propose a way to
[L149] understand phenomenologically the emergence of the ef￾fective Lorentzian dynamics. It is however to be remem￾bered that there is no dynamics at the fundamental level
[L150] and that this illusion is restricted to a domain of a large
[L151] Euclidean space.

[L887] G. Discussion
[L888] This section has provided the general construction of a
[L889] mechanism that allows for scalar, vector, and spinor fields
[L890] to actually propagate in an effective Lorentzian metric
[L891] even though the underlying theory is purely Euclidean
[L892] and written in terms of the Euclidean metric δµν. This
[L893] general construction assumes the existence of a scalar
[L894] field φ, called clock field, that couples to all fields (scalar,
[L895] vector and spinor fields). In particular, this implies that
[L896] we can construct the whole standard model of particle
[L897] physics.
[L898] Let us now discuss some properties and limitations of
[L899] such a construction.
